articles.headline: Lugo estrena su estación intermodal tras años de espera y con la demanda de más trenes
articles.subtitle: La terminal ferroviaria abrió este martes sin acto inaugural y con la estación de autobuses todavía sin fecha, mientras los viajeros reclaman frecuencias y tiempos de viaje más cortos
articles.body:
La nueva estación de tren de Lugo abrió este martes sus puertas y registró catorce movimientos de convoyes en su primer día de servicio, según el recuento de El Progreso. La terminal, situada en la Rúa Alta-Plaza Conde de Fontao, sustituye a la antigua y forma parte de un área intermodal cuya estación de autobuses aún no tiene fecha de apertura.

La puesta en servicio se produjo sin acto inaugural, coincidiendo con la campaña electoral del 29N. Adif ejecutó la obra con el Ayuntamiento sobre un proyecto que estuvo paralizado durante años y que incluye un edificio de viajeros de dos plantas, nuevos andenes y marquesinas, un paso inferior de uso mixto y una pasarela peatonal hacia la terminal de autobuses.

## Las cifras no cuadran entre las fuentes

El coste depende de dónde se ponga el límite. El Progreso cifra las obras de la estación en 22,3 millones y eleva la cuenta a 49 millones al sumar las actuaciones vinculadas a la estación de autobuses. La Voz de Galicia habla de una inversión de 23 millones. La Región atribuye al conjunto ejecutado por Adif un coste superior a los 49 millones.

La oferta de trenes, en cambio, no cambió. La Voz de Galicia sostiene que solo seis convoyes al día están en servicio; su crónica resume la queja de los primeros viajeros en el titular: «Es muy amplia, pero necesitamos trenes». Fernando Carballal, usuario habitual, fue más lejos: «Hace muchos años había mejores comunicaciones que ahora».

Quedan además obras pendientes: el llamado paso de ciudad, con ascensores y rampas hacia la Ronda da Muralla; la electrificación completa de la vía y la eliminación de pasos a nivel, que mantiene algunos trayectos en autobús; la modernización de las líneas a A Coruña y Ourense; y la conexión directa con Santiago, una reivindicación histórica sin resolver.

articles.headline: Un boleto sellado en Outeiro de Rei reparte un millón de euros de El Millón
articles.subtitle: El restaurante González, en San Martiño de Guillar, validó el boleto premiado del sorteo del martes y su dueño dice que no sabe quién es el afortunado entre una clientela de paso y de la zona
articles.body:
El despacho de loterías del restaurante González, en San Martiño de Guillar, en el municipio de Outeiro de Rei, validó el boleto de El Millón agraciado con un millón de euros en el sorteo de Euromillones celebrado el martes por la noche. El local, que también tiene pensión, está a pie de la N-6, en el límite entre Lugo y Outeiro.

Óscar Vilaboa, responsable del negocio, se enteró pocos minutos después de las 22.15 horas. «Acaban de comunicarnos la noticia desde Loterías», contó a El Progreso. Se mostró sorprendido porque, aunque en alguna ocasión habían repartido premios altos, nunca una cantidad así: «Alguna vez repartimos premios superiores, pero como este, ninguno».

El hostelero cree que será difícil identificar al ganador, ya que por el restaurante pasan tanto clientes de la zona como viajeros que paran de camino. El código del boleto premiado es HRP50707. Los responsables del local esperan, dijeron, que haya ido a parar «a alguien que lo necesite».

El sorteo no dejó acertantes de primera categoría, de modo que el bote sube a 59 millones para el sorteo del viernes. La combinación ganadora fue 03, 05, 37, 44 y 49, con las estrellas 05 y 06. Hubo un acertante de segunda categoría, que cobrará 486.463,07 euros, y diez de cuarta, con 14.910,75 euros cada uno. La recaudación total ascendió a 37,27 millones.

Lugo repite suerte en El Millón. En febrero de 2025 el Bar Madeira, en Fontiñas, vendió otro boleto premiado con la misma cantidad, y años antes lo había hecho un supermercado de Triacastela.

articles.headline: El Hierro roza en un mes tantos migrantes como habitantes: 11.782 llegadas en 24 días
articles.subtitle: El muelle de La Restinga concentra casi el 60% de las entradas del año y el centro de acogida de Valverde se queda corto, mientras Canarias reclama al Gobierno que blinde la derivación de menores
articles.body:
El puerto de La Restinga, en El Hierro, ha recibido 11.782 migrantes en los primeros 24 días de noviembre, una cifra equivalente al 97,82% de los 12.000 habitantes censados en la isla, según el recuento de El Mundo. Solo cuatro jornadas del mes han transcurrido sin la llegada de un cayuco.

El lunes desembarcaron 1.282 personas —71 de ellas menores— en ocho embarcaciones pesqueras, y una novena se aproximaba a la isla al cierre de la edición. En lo que va de año la isla suma 19.795 llegadas, y el muelle de La Restinga, un pueblo de 673 vecinos, ha concentrado el 59,52% de ellas.

2026 se perfila como el segundo año de mayor presión de la serie histórica, solo por detrás de 2024, cuando llegaron 23.994 personas, casi el doble de la población censada. RTVE cifraba en casi 11.000 los migrantes llegados en todo noviembre al cierre del domingo, con Senegal, Gambia y Guinea Conakry como principales países de origen.

## La saturación asistencial

El Centro de Atención Temporal de Extranjeros (CATE) de Valverde, con 800 plazas pendientes todavía de reforma y una decena escasa de agentes de la Policía Nacional, se ha quedado corto ante el ritmo de los desembarcos: obligó a instalar carpas anexas y dejó imágenes de personas durmiendo de madrugada en los asientos del puerto de La Estaca a la espera de ferri.

El presidente canario, Fernando Clavijo, exigió el lunes al Ejecutivo que el último Consejo de Ministros blindase la modificación del artículo 35 de la Ley de Extranjería para que la derivación de menores no dependa de que se renueve cada año. La Comisión Interministerial de Migraciones decretó la emergencia migratoria en Canarias con una dotación inicial de unos 15 millones de euros.

articles.headline: Los decretos electorales de Sánchez dejan casi 22.000 millones de factura al próximo Gobierno
articles.subtitle: El último Consejo de Ministros aprueba un paquete de unos 2.000 millones, con 1.200 para prorrogar las ayudas al transporte, mientras la patronal pide derogar lo aprobado en campaña
articles.body:
El Gobierno que salga de las urnas el domingo tendrá que afrontar una factura de gasto extraordinario cercana a los 22.000 millones de euros por el conjunto de medidas sociales que Pedro Sánchez ha aprobado durante la campaña, según los cálculos que publica El Mundo. Muchas son mejoras retributivas, ampliaciones de permisos y rebajas fiscales difíciles de revertir.

Solo el paquete aprobado en el último Consejo de Ministros, celebrado el martes, ronda los 2.000 millones. El grueso —más de 1.200 millones— corresponde a la prórroga de las ayudas al transporte público durante 2027, con los descuentos actuales en vigor.

El Ejecutivo amplió el permiso por nacimiento o cuidado del menor de 19 a 20 semanas, con un coste estimado de unos 300 millones, y elevó a diez días el permiso por fallecimiento de un familiar, que en este caso asumirán las empresas. Añadió una rebaja del IRPF para 2,6 millones de autónomos valorada en 465 millones y un régimen voluntario para declarar el IVA una sola vez al año si se factura menos de 85.000 euros.

A esa traca final se suman la revalorización de las pensiones y la subida salarial de los funcionarios, con un coste conjunto de unos 17.600 millones: 8.400 por el alza previsto del 3,6% en las nóminas de los pensionistas y 9.200 por el 4,5% pactado con los empleados públicos más un 0,5% adicional por el exceso de inflación de este año.

La portavoz del Gobierno, Elma Saiz, defendió las normas porque se dirigen «al 100% de la ciudadanía» con independencia de su ideología, y alegó que las rebajas fiscales a los autónomos deben estar en vigor antes del 1 de enero, según Europa Press. La CEOE ha pedido públicamente al próximo Ejecutivo que dé de baja todas las medidas aprobadas en las últimas semanas.

articles.headline: El Supremo avala el DNI digital para votar el 29N y rechaza el recurso contra las urnas de cartón
articles.subtitle: La Sala de lo Contencioso da por cumplidos los controles de seguridad de MiDNI y remite a la Junta Electoral Central la disputa sobre el voto de los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos
articles.body:
El Tribunal Supremo ha avalado el uso del DNI electrónico con el sistema MiDNI como medio de identificación en las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre y ha desestimado el recurso de Iustitia Europa, que pedía suspenderlo, según el auto difundido por Europa Press y ABC.

El alto tribunal había reclamado al Ministerio del Interior las certificaciones de seguridad del sistema y concluye que esos controles «han sido cumplidos». Añade que «no existe un riesgo serio, real y fundado» de que los dispositivos que decodifican los códigos QR se vean afectados por causas ajenas a su funcionamiento normal.

Suspender la medida, razona la Sala, resultaría «desproporcionada» para el fin constitucionalmente legítimo de identificar a cada votante si el argumento es la falta de un protocolo uniforme ante incidencias.

En la misma resolución el tribunal rechaza un recurso contra el uso de urnas de cartón y mesas específicas en los consulados para los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos, cuyo voto sigue suspendido cautelarmente salvo que acrediten determinados requisitos. La Región precisa que el Supremo no entró a valorar la idoneidad de esos materiales y remitió la cuestión a la Junta Electoral Central, competente para resolverla.

La controversia afecta a más de 160.000 personas nacionalizadas mediante la ley de nietos y entró en la campaña electoral después de que se difundieran imágenes de esas urnas en los consulados.

articles.headline: Burnham turns down Stormont leaders' request for a meeting on the budget
articles.subtitle: Northern Ireland's first and deputy first ministers sought direct engagement to break a seven-month impasse; the prime minister is backing the NI secretary to keep leading the talks
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has declined a request from Northern Ireland's first and deputy first ministers to meet him over Stormont's budget stalemate. Michelle O'Neill and Emma Little-Pengelly had jointly written to the prime minister seeking direct engagement in an attempt to resolve an impasse that is now more than seven months into the financial year.

It is understood the prime minister has backed Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant to continue leading talks on the government's behalf. Burnham is said to be urging the Stormont executive to accept the offer of an extra £1.5bn over the next three years and finalise a financial plan.

No budget has been agreed by the four-party coalition. Departments have been operating under contingency arrangements that let them spend up to 95% of last year's funding, and ministers have insisted the additional money does not go far enough to let them set a budget.

The News Letter reports that the executive met on Tuesday morning and, in O'Neill's words, had a "good discussion" and "remain of one mind" on the funding shortfall. About £525m of the £1.5bn would arrive this year. Last month's UK Budget allocated a further £131m for the current financial year and £270m across three years. Trade unions have warned of widespread strikes if public sector pay is not delivered.

The first minister had asked her DUP counterpart to join the approach, saying it would be a "dereliction of responsibility" for Little-Pengelly to refuse. Both parties sit in the same executive and, seven months on, are still making the same argument to London rather than to each other.

articles.headline: Leaked Russian data points to nearly half a million soldiers dead in Ukraine
articles.subtitle: BBC Russian and Mediazona counted at least 490,334 deaths in records hacked from Rosstat, while independent Russian outlets put total losses above 700,000 including the missing
articles.body:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by BBC Russian and the independent outlet Mediazona. The figure comes from more than 11 million death records covering 2021 to September 2026, obtained after a hack that Russia's statistics agency, Rosstat, acknowledged while denying that protected information had leaked.

The Belarusian group Cyber Partisans and Ukraine's Silent Crow are reported to have carried out the breach. BBC Russian matched the Rosstat records against its own list of confirmed military deaths drawn from open sources and found matches for 90% of them.

The data shows how the war has reshaped mortality in Russia. Of Russians aged 18 to 24 who died in 2025, 65% were killed in the war; among those aged 25 to 34 the share was 59%. Only in the 45 to 54 bracket does cardiovascular disease claim more lives than the conflict. About 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for ten Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

The total is contested. Meduza and Mediazona published a separate estimate on Monday putting Russian military deaths above 700,000, calculated from the same leaked trove and adjusted for the lag with which deaths reach the state system, which does not yet record most of 2026. France 24 reported the same figure as losses including the missing. The Kremlin has never published a death toll for the war.

articles.headline: Amnesty asks the ICC to examine genocide claims over births in Gaza
articles.subtitle: The rights group says Israeli measures prevented births and damaged women's reproductive health, as Israeli strikes killed Hamas's internal security chief and at least four others
articles.body:
Amnesty International has urged the International Criminal Court to investigate whether Israeli officials committed genocide in Gaza, citing measures it says prevented births and severely damaged women's reproductive health. The report was published on Wednesday, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.

Amnesty's secretary general, Agnès Callamard, said that from October 2023 until October 2026 "Israel's actions have prevented access to fertility treatment and contributed to pregnancy complications, including miscarriage and stillbirth". The organisation said it had serious concerns that the effects were intentional, while acknowledging it could not reach a definitive conclusion.

The report says Gaza had at least nine clinics offering IVF before the war and that none now provide the treatment, with thousands of stored embryos, sperm and eggs destroyed. Amnesty said it found evidence that Palestinian armed groups used hospitals to hold hostages and to torture Palestinians, but no evidence supporting Israeli claims that they were used as Hamas command centres.

## A security chief killed

In Gaza, an Israeli air strike killed Naeem Abu Nahel, head of Hamas's internal security service. The Hamas-run interior ministry said the 50-year-old, in the post only since September, was targeted in western Gaza City, and Benjamin Netanyahu and defence minister Israel Katz announced he had been "eliminated".

Al Jazeera reported at least four people killed in a strike on an apartment building in the Shati refugee camp. Palestinian medics said six others died in two strikes on Tuesday, including a teenage boy and two police officers. Strikes have continued almost daily despite the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October last year.

articles.headline: Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four colleagues over hijab-less concert
articles.subtitle: A defence lawyer told the BBC that Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer each received 74 lashes in Qom, two years after her livestreamed performance was seen around the world
articles.body:
Iranian authorities have flogged the singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her band and production team, according to their defence lawyers. Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer each received 74 lashes at the criminal sentence enforcement office in the city of Qom, one of the lawyers told the BBC on Monday.

The case dates from December 2024, when Ahmadi performed in a sleeveless dress in a concert livestreamed on her YouTube channel. Iranian law bans public performances by women and requires them to wear the headscarf and modest clothing. The video circulated widely online.

In June a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through publishing "obscene and indecent material", charges they denied. Alongside the 74 lashes they were banned from audiovisual work and from leaving Iran for two years. At the end of September an appeals court in Qom rejected their appeal and upheld the sentence.

The sentences drew condemnation from Iranian artists and human rights activists, who argued that flogging is cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment and breaches the international prohibition on torture. France 24 reported that the United Nations also criticised Iran over the case. Ahmadi's lawyers confirmed the flogging four days after the punishment was carried out.

articles.headline: Ábrego García leaves the US for Spain after a year and a half of legal battle
articles.subtitle: The Salvadoran whose mistaken deportation to El Salvador became a symbol of Trump's immigration drive has flown to Spain, which his lawyer describes as a temporary departure
articles.body:
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador last year turned him into a symbol of the fight over Donald Trump's immigration policy, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday. He took a commercial flight, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Ábrego García is Salvadoran and had lived in Maryland for years after arriving illegally as a teenager. In 2019 an immigration judge ruled that he could not be sent back to El Salvador because of danger from a gang that had threatened his family, and allowed him to live and work in the US under supervision, without residency status.

The administration admitted in 2025 that it had deported him in error, brought him back to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped, and then pressed to send him to countries including Uganda, Ghana and Liberia. A judge told him on Tuesday to self-deport, the Associated Press reported, after a memo noted a US agreement with Costa Rica to take deportees who cannot legally be returned home.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat who visited him in El Salvador's Cecot prison, said he was travelling "to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity". His lawyer said the departure was "temporary" and that he had "many options to return", adding that the family expected a future administration to bring him back to Maryland.

articles.headline: Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets but cleared of racketeering in Brooklyn trial
articles.subtitle: Jurors convicted the Chinese telecoms giant on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to violate US sanctions; sentencing is set for September 2027 and an appeal is expected
articles.body:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge, in a landmark trial at Brooklyn federal court. Jurors convicted the Chinese technology and telecoms giant on 10 of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

Over two months prosecutors accused Huawei of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage, including misleading banks about its business dealings in Iran. The defence argued the government had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and then built its case around that conclusion, and that the company's success came from its own innovation.

The charges were first announced in 2019, after the arrest a year earlier of Huawei's finance chief, Meng Wanzhou, in Canada at the request of US authorities. She was held for three years before being released to return to China under a deal with US prosecutors.

The racketeering count required jurors to find that the firm acted as a criminal enterprise. Huawei said the acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years". Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027; defence lawyer Brian Heberlig said there would be "significant advocacy" to secure the lowest sentence possible, and that he fully expects an appeal. "If I know Huawei, that fight will continue," he said.

articles.headline: Uber, Nuro and Lucid start fully driverless robotaxi testing in the Bay Area
articles.subtitle: The Lucid Gravity fleet is running without a safety driver in four Silicon Valley cities, but the public launch has slipped from 2026 to the first quarter of 2027
articles.body:
Uber, Nuro and Lucid have begun testing robotaxis with nobody in the driver's seat on public roads around Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos and Sunnyvale, the companies announced on 24 November. Rides for employees are due to start soon, and the service is expected to open in the Uber app in the first quarter of 2027, later than the 2026 launch the partners had promised.

The vehicles are Lucid Gravity SUVs fitted with high-resolution cameras, lidar and radar, running Nuro's end-to-end Nuro Driver system. Lucid says the robotaxi fleet already numbers about 100 vehicles, built at its Arizona factory, and the road testing will expand to more Bay Area cities next year.

Uber has committed to buying 35,000 Lucid-Nuro robotaxis and plans to operate them in dozens of markets, with Houston named as the second city for mid-2027. Uber's chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, told investors on the third-quarter call that the Bay Area service would run "fully driverless from day one".

Testing is not the same as charging passengers. The announcement references a California Public Utilities Commission drivered pilot permit, which allows passengers only with a safety operator aboard; carrying paying riders without one needs further approvals, and the companies have not said which permits they will hold at launch. California's DMV list does include a Nuro entry for driverless testing in Santa Clara and San Mateo counties, at speeds of 25 to 45mph depending on the permit.

articles.headline: US suspects Iran behind cyberattacks on dozens of tankers at sea
articles.subtitle: As many as 50 shipping vessels carrying oil and gas were breached across Asia and Europe, according to a report, prompting FBI and Coast Guard boarding teams in August
articles.body:
US officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks on shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by TechCrunch. The ships, carrying oil, liquefied gas and other explosive chemicals, were hacked as they travelled across Asia and Europe.

In August, several oil tankers heading towards the US coast also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cyber teams from the FBI and the Coast Guard to board the vessels. Officials are investigating whether Iran is widening its campaign against the US by targeting large ships to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or try to cause an explosion at a port. Vessels retain backup controls when automated systems are hacked or fail.

Attention has focused on a flaw dubbed FortiBleed, which lets attackers break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet routers, hardware used on many ships. A joint FBI and Coast Guard alert in September warned that shipping operators run Fortinet equipment and that the bug was being exploited in the wild.

Iran has struck out in several directions since the US and Israel went to war with it earlier this year, and much of its retaliation has been digital: US officials have blamed Tehran for hacks on hundreds of water providers and on medical technology companies. The FBI did not respond to a request for comment on the shipping attacks or on whether it has a more accurate figure than 50.

articles.headline: Two unsecured databases exposed 3.6 billion logins, documents and ID numbers
articles.subtitle: A researcher found credentials in plaintext for services including Google, Facebook, X and Amazon, alongside hundreds of thousands of files lifted from infected machines
articles.body:
Security researchers have unearthed two unsecured databases holding more than 3.6 billion records, including usernames, passwords, documents and national identity numbers, Wired reported. Jeremiah Fowler of Black Hills Information Security found one of them, containing roughly two billion login credentials.

Fowler said the logins were "associated with virtually every type of online service imaginable": hundreds of millions of email accounts, more than 100 million social media accounts and tens of millions of shopping accounts. The estimated totals include 114 million accounts linked to Google services, 88 million on Facebook, nearly 33 million on X, almost 42 million on Roblox and 36.6 million on Amazon, though there may be overlap between services and individual users.

Thousands of folders held credentials in plaintext, sorted by country with the US, UK, France and Germany among those named. About 400,000 documents appeared to come from more advanced malware that created a separate folder for each victim, with files labelled clipboard, cookies, brute force, passwords and system.

"Together, these could provide a detailed profile of each victim and their devices and accounts," Fowler wrote in a research post for ExpressVPN, adding that it would open "a much wider range of potential attack paths".

He was blunter with Wired. "If you had that, you own that person," he said. The practical defence is unchanged: unique passwords for every service, stored in a password manager, plus passkeys or multi-factor authentication wherever they are offered.

articles.headline: Check Point security servers compromised at 22 organisations in 17 countries
articles.subtitle: GreyNoise traced the campaign, tracked as GT13, from 17 October and says the intruders kept persistent access, suggesting it is still running
articles.body:
Threat actors have exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise Check Point security management servers at 22 organisations across 17 countries in a campaign that carries the hallmarks of cyberespionage. Threat intelligence firm GreyNoise detected the activity, tracked as GT13, and says it could not conclusively determine the attacker's motive.

GreyNoise confirmed the campaign ran between 17 October and 2 November, when its own visibility ended, but believes it is still active given how persistently the intruders held access to the devices. The victims include government entities, financial services providers and companies in the energy, transportation, mining and manufacturing sectors, with no clear evidence of targeting along any single line.

The attacks came from 99 IP addresses that appear to be compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. A Rejetto HTTP file server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data.

GreyNoise could not establish how or when the servers were first breached, but observed exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during later stages. That is an authentication bypass in Check Point's SmartConsole that lets attackers obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges; Check Point warned about it in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day.

articles.headline: Hackers' AI agents found and exploited a zero-day with almost no human help, Amazon says
articles.subtitle: The agents were handed a list of IP addresses and one instruction — get shell access — and then broke into an East Asian university server running medical imaging software
articles.body:
Amazon says AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a short instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework.

The attackers wrote prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to Chinese Standard Time, then supplied a list of IP addresses with one goal: "obtain shell access". In short order the agents found a zero-day in an open-source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers, exploited it and took full control of the system.

Cairn is an open-source problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. A dispatcher reads a shared graph of facts and hints, schedules tasks and assigns each project to worker containers that run several agents concurrently. It is model-agnostic, running on backends including Claude Code, Codex and Pi, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 has seen it driven by GLM 5.2 and by DeepSeek V4 Flash and V4 Pro.

Amazon's security team warned that "agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable". Unit 42 reported earlier this month that attackers had used Cairn against semiconductor, defence and civil society organisations, running 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 of them; at least 10 were successfully breached.

articles.headline: Tidal will delete 27 million AI-generated tracks on 9 December
articles.subtitle: The streaming service says 43% of everything uploaded in the past 90 days was made entirely by AI, and that 96% of the tracks it will wipe were never played
articles.body:
Tidal has said it will ban music created entirely by AI and delete the 27 million tracks already labelled that way, abandoning the labelling approach most streaming services have settled on. The company made the announcement on its own account on X, and the deletion is set for 9 December.

Tidal introduced a policy in July 2026 that labelled and demonetised fully AI-made songs. That was not enough. Over the past 90 days, Tidal says 43% of new uploads were completely AI-generated; on 6 November the share reached 60%. The 27 million AI-labelled tracks make up 6.3% of the catalogue and were almost all uploaded in the past two years.

The company argues the harm to human artists outweighs the loss, noting that 96% of the AI-labelled tracks had zero plays in the past 90 days. It also says some AI uploaders are actively trying to siphon royalty payments, and that it has already removed about 66,000 tracks for impersonating other artists, which breached its rules even before this change.

Artists will still be allowed to use AI tools as long as the finished work contains human elements — the ban covers only music that is fully machine-made. TechCrunch reports that AI-generated material has been flooding every major streaming platform, and that Tidal concluded labelling had failed to slow it down.

articles.headline: Anthropic's shares fall below the IPO price days after a record debut
articles.subtitle: The Claude maker is now worth less than $1.2tn, more than 30% below its peak, in a selloff that has dragged chip stocks and the Nasdaq down with it
articles.body:
Anthropic's shares have fallen below their $83 offer price, less than a week after a debut that briefly valued the Claude developer at $2tn. The stock opened at $111.50 on its first day of trading, touched $115.10 and closed at $97.17; it has fallen every session since.

The slide has erased most of the first-day gain and left a market capitalisation just under $1.2tn. At roughly 30 times trailing sales, the valuation leaves almost no room for disappointment. The selloff has pulled chip stocks and the Nasdaq with it, and the index has now given back its gains for 2026.

TechCrunch calls the drop a worrying sign for AI startups, and the timing matters: OpenAI is not expected to list before 2027. Bloomberg ran a markets segment titled "Anthropic IPO Could Mark End of the AI Trade", reviving the old suspicion that the biggest listing of a boom tends to arrive near the top. Analysts quoted by Reuters had hoped the IPO would be a "clearing event" for AI stocks; it was not.

One detail did not help sentiment. Dario and Daniela Amodei, the company's chief executive and president, each disclosed the sale of roughly $280m of shares as part of the offering. The shares went to underwriters at the offer price rather than being dumped on the market, but the optics in a week like this are poor.

articles.headline: OpenRouter drops three AI providers after prompts and secrets leaked to third parties
articles.subtitle: Dragos pushed two million test prompts carrying decoy credentials through the gateway and found live keys being used against controlled AWS accounts
articles.body:
OpenRouter, the gateway that routes developer requests to dozens of AI models, has removed three inference providers after a security firm found evidence that prompts and embedded credentials were reaching parties customers never expected to see them.

Dragos sent two million test prompts through the platform, each carrying a unique tracking link or a decoy credential, and detected "activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed". OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached, which points at the provider layer. The providers removed are Together AI, Phala and Novita.

The Hacker News reports that the exposure ran from May to November 2026 and covers application secrets and AWS keys written into prompts, system prompts containing proprietary business logic, and — for Phala — user requests to DeepSeek's V4 Flash model between 21 October and 8 November. Any key, token or password inside those requests should be treated as compromised and rotated.

A fourth provider, Atlas Cloud, said it would withdraw its models voluntarily pending security testing. OpenRouter has revoked zero-data-retention eligibility for 125 endpoints and will keep running Dragos-style checks, including whether providers forward requests or responses to third parties, before restoring it. The researchers say planted keys and links were still being accessed months after the first thefts.
